content:
An investigation into four of the most common AI platforms found that the programs can help everyday users plan and execute “verified, feasible attacks” on national security or the U.S. economy, and that the platforms’ internal safeguards can easily be bypassed.

Prompts to Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini this past spring resulted in the programs generating detailed attack plans in less than 12 hours when asked. The plans listed specific targets, locations, timing, attack methods, and ways to avoid detection, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) said in a report released publicly on Wednesday.

While generative AI is credited with decreasing the amount of time needed to perform many tasks, the GAO warns that these results show that it’s also capable of serious harm by an everyday, average user.

“These advancements are enabling malicious actors to pursue nefarious actions faster and more efficiently and empowering less-skilled individuals by filling knowledge gaps through providing detailed expertise in sensitive areas,” the report states.

“Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans; however, the amount of time to get results could vary for many reasons, including the topic and user experience,” it added.

The findings were presented to the Congressional Joint Economic Committee (JEC) in October, before being publicly released this week.

All four platforms were also presented with the findings and “generally stated that their companies will continue to improve the safety of their platforms,” according to the report.

A spokesperson for ChatGPT maker OpenAI told HuffPost that the tests were done using an older model of its program and that “considerable safety improvements” have been made since.

“We rigorously test our safeguards internally and with external experts, and we use monitoring, human review and enforcement to identify and address misuse and strengthen our protections,” the spokesperson added.

The researchers at GAO said they independently verified that the information provided by each of the four AI platforms was sufficient for a user to plan and execute an attack.

In one instance, the GAO said they consulted a bomb squad commander at a fire department in a major metropolitan area who confirmed that plans shared for making an improvised explosive device would result in an explosion. They also visited the AI’s suggested locations for purchasing the materials, confirmed the materials’ availability, and visited the targeted location on the suggested date of the attack.

“While there, we noted conditions that, with minor tweaks, could have allowed a malicious actor to inflict increased harm, including casualties,” the report states.

In another planned IED attack example, an AI platform offered guidance on purchasing materials, cleaning evidence, renting a catering vehicle, leasing property, and opening a shell company to avoid suspicion and detection.

All four platforms did activate guardrails in the process of the malicious prompts, like denying requests and suspending the user’s account, but the GAO said they were able to bypass the safety guardrails each time.

Sen. Margaret Hassan (D-N.H.), who requested the report as ranking member of the JEC, said the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee will review these and other AI threats during its first meeting next year, with her as the committee’s incoming chair.

“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” she said in a statement Wednesday.
